articles.title: Can pancreatic cancer be stopped in its tracks? Radical tactic raises hopes
articles.description: With prospects for new treatments at an all-time high, researchers are looking for ways to boost survival by treating the disease early.
articles.body:
Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research Early detection of pancreatic cancer (red; artificially coloured) could help to improve the survival rates of a highly lethal disease. Credit: PDC/SPL
Armed with new tools and fresh optimism , researchers seeking to subdue pancreatic cancer — one of the world’s deadliest — are chasing a radical strategy: cancer interception .
In this approach, tissues that are growing abnormally are treated to keep them from turning cancerous and spreading. Interception is already being trialled for breast and skin cancers , among others. But now the success of a new drug that quashes pancreatic tumours is raising scientists’ hopes that interception could succeed even for this recalcitrant cancer.
CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

articles.title: Prozac use for childhood depression skewed by single flawed medical trial
articles.description: One small study in Iran swayed meta-analyses in favour of antidepressant use in children, researchers say.
articles.body:
Richard Van Noorden is a features editor at Nature in London.
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research The medication fluoxetine, sold under the brand name Prozac, is recommended as a treatment for depression in children and adolescents in several clinical guidelines. Credit: Jb Reed/Bloomberg via Getty
A single clinical trial of 40 children in Iran, published in 2006, might have wrongly swayed medical evidence in favour of using Prozac (fluoxetine) to treat depression in children and adolescents, a group of researchers say. They’re now calling that trial’s findings into question and suggest that, in their opinion, Prozac’s recommendation in paediatric clinical guidelines isn’t sufficiently supported by the evidence — although they stop short of calling for clinicians to stop prescribing Prozac for depression in children.
Instead, “guideline committees should review their recommendations, acknowledge the evidence we have clarified and go through their process of weighing up whether use can still be justified”, says Richard Lyus, a consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist in Cambridge, UK, and a co-author of the study, which was published this month in Cochrane Evidence Synthesis and Methods 1 .
The finding shows how a single ‘zombie’ trial — that is, one with data so flawed as to be untrustworthy — can corrupt the evidence base for a front-line medical treatment, says Florian Naudet, a psychiatrist at the University of Rennes in France, and another co-author of the study.
Scientists have repeatedly warned that flawed studies are affecting the results of systematic reviews in medicine and other fields , but it’s rare to find such a clear example, Naudet says.
The researchers who conducted the controversial trial did not respond to repeated e-mail enquiries from Naudet’s team and did not contact him or his colleagues when they posted a preprint on the server medRxiv describing their analysis in September last year; nor did they respond to Nature ’s request for comment.
Prozac is one of the most frequently prescribed antidepressants in children. Many national prescribing guidelines recommend the drug on the basis of a 2016 meta-analysis published in The Lancet 2 , which found that Prozac is better than placebo for treating depression in children and adolescents. A 2020 meta-analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry supported those findings 3 . But in 2021, a meta-analysis published in Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 4 found that Prozac had only a ‘small and unimportant’ advantage over placebo, and that it was probably no better than other antidepressants.
Giant study finds untrustworthy trials pollute gold-standard medical reviews

articles.title: Sugar-rich foods exacerbate antibiotic-induced microbiome disruption - Nature
articles.description: Avoiding a diet rich in simple sugars during treatment with antibiotics may mitigate microbiota disruption.
articles.body: Diet shapes the composition of the gut microbiota 1 ; however, the specific effects of distinct food groups on microbiome dynamics are unclear, particularly in circumstances of extreme perturbation. Here we evaluated the relationship between diet and intestinal microbiome dynamics by precisely tracking 9,419 meals consumed by 173 patients who were hospitalized for haematopoietic cell transplantation and analysing subsequent microbiome changes. Bayesian inference applied to data from 158 patients with paired longitudinal microbiome samples revealed that the intake of sweets and sugars during antibiotic exposure predicted exacerbated microbial dysbiosis, manifesting as lowered α-diversity and greater expansion of the pathobiont Enterococcus . Experiments in mice also showed that sucrose supplementation increased and prolonged antibiotic-induced Enterococcus expansion. These data suggest that avoiding a diet rich in simple sugars during antibiotic treatment may mitigate microbiota disruption. Further studies in independent cohorts will offer opportunities to generalize these findings and evaluate microbiota-sparing interventions.

articles.title: Daily briefing: How to save corals from the El Niño
articles.description: Scientists are trying to help coral reefs survive record ocean temperatures. Plus, the aftermath of a deadly attack on Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and whether it’s OK to dodge small talk.
articles.body:
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Sign up for Nature Briefing Save article View saved research Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here .
Coral reefs in the Philippines are still recovering from the last El Niño, even as another one gains strength. Credit: Alex Mustard/Nature Picture Library
Scientists warn we’re headed for a mass coral bleaching event around the globe, just a few years after the last coral crisis. Researchers working on coral restoration are doing what they can to help reefs survive and recover from record ocean temperatures. Approaches include breeding corals with improved tolerance to heat and acidity; treating corals with microbial cocktails and micronutrients; and luring coral larvae by playing the underwater sounds of a healthy reef. But these small-scale wins can only succeed alongside reductions in greenhouse-gas emissions, overfishing and pollution.
People were cut off by the flames and forced to escape through the windows of the Presidium building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. (Volodymyr Tarasov/Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty )
Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences has called for the global community to continue to shun Russian state scientific and educational institutions after Russia destroyed the society’s building in central Kyiv, killing two people , on Monday. “There can be no ‘science is above politics’ when science is under armed attacks,” the academy said.
Times Higher Education | 5 min read (free reg required) & Science | 6 min read
Reference: National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine statement
The OpenAI Foundation — the charity arm of the artificial-intelligence behemoth — is on track to become one of the wealthiest non-profit organizations on the planet. It has so far funded Alzheimer’s disease research, cancer vaccines and a pilot project to repurpose data from bankrupt biotechnology companies. “Part of the reason that we’re starting in the life sciences and health is that we think that’s one of the areas where AI can have the most benefit,” says Jacob Trefethen , who leads life sciences at the foundation.
The fearsome Tyrannosaurus rex might have had an internal body temperature similar to that of modern-day elephants — and not too dissimilar to humans. By examining the arrangement of isotopes in the enamel of fossilized T. rex teeth, researchers estimate that the dinosaur’s internal temperature was approximately 36 °C . Narrowing down the creature’s body temperature can hint at what kind of diet it needed to sustain its homeostasis, and where it was able to roam.
The vocalizations of the common marmoset ( Callithrix jacchus ), the olive colobus monkey ( Procolobus verus ) and the bonobo ( Pan paniscus ) all appear to contain patterns that resemble complex elements of human grammar . Researchers used mathematical models to analyse clips of these monkey’s communications and identified some elements similar to supra-regular recursion — a grammatical structure that requires a listener to process a word or statement nested within a wider sentence without context. This level of complexity was thought to be unique to humans.
Reference: bioRxiv preprint (not peer reviewed)
A scientist with no appetite for small talk asks: is it OK to arrive late to meetings to avoid it, and to cut it off quickly when they’re the one in charge? A panel of Nature readers gave their judgement — read on to see if you agree .
Three researchers respond to a Nature Careers advice column about a PhD student who was distressed by killing research animals. They argue that, rather than offering coping mechanisms, the article could have suggested discussing possible adjustments with supervisors and considering responsible dissent. ( Nature | 3 min read )

articles.title: Stunning fossil shows dinosaurs’ distinctive path to flight
articles.description: A fossil from a previously undiscovered species with feathery limbs, unearthed in China, adds to evidence that dinosaurs and birds evolved flight more than once.
articles.body:
Sarah Wild is a freelance journalist in Canterbury, UK.
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research The Norellraptor barsboldi fossil shows traces of feathers on its fore and hind limbs as well as at the end of its tail. Credit: Xuri Wang et al./Nat. Commun .
The discovery of a species of feathered dinosaur in China, through a stunningly well-preserved fossil, adds to a growing body of evidence that birds and their closest relatives evolved the ability to fly several times rather than through a single lineage.
The specimen, which is 57 centimetres long, is a microraptorine that roamed what is now Liaoning province in China between 145 million and 100 million years ago. It was discovered by a local farmer and described by an international team of researchers from China, Italy and Slovakia in Nature Communications on 29 September 1 . The team named the species Norellraptor barsboldi and estimate that the specimen would have been about three years old when it died.
Microraptorines are a group of relatively small meat-eating dinosaurs, weighing around one kilogram, that had feathers on their limbs. Hundreds of specimens have been found. The feathered creatures are part of a complete branch, or clade, of the tree of life called Microraptorinae. They are close relatives to birds, which are part of the Avialae clade, and so they offer insight into the origins and evolution of flight.
By comparing the flight-related adaptations of known microraptorines with those observed in the bird lineage, the researchers found that 30% of the 194 flight-related adaptations identified in microraptorines also evolved in the Avialae. These include wing feathers, hook-shaped toe bones and a longer bone in the forearm than in the upper arm.
This miniature skull belonged to a 2-gram dinosaur

articles.title: Nature has rights — it is time the world recognized them
articles.description: Existing legal frameworks have not halted planetary crises. Recognizing the rights of nature could offer a different path.
articles.body:
Juan Carlos Navarro is minister of the environment of the Republic of Panama in Panama City, Panama.
Callie Veelenturf is a marine biologist in Panama City, Panama, at the UN Harmony with Nature programme in New York City, New York, USA, a National Geographic Explorer and founder of the non-profit organization forNature.
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research The natural world has too few legal protections. Credit: Damocean/Getty
Wildfires, heatwaves and unprecedented weather events are no longer breaking news, they’re our permanent backdrop. Yet again this year, we are facing the grave effects of a climate system that we have destabilized. We are watching the world experience painful and deadly climate extremes, while our collective response remains ‘too little, too late’.
Although we’re in need of hope, hope is never a plan. As a global society and as citizens of Earth, we urgently need a tangible shift in how our legal systems treat the living world. Recognizing the universal rights of nature is the answer.
Why environmental treaties must also address mental health

articles.title: Can you name the women who have won a science Nobel prize?
articles.description: Take Nature’s quiz on female Nobel laureates in physics, chemistry or physiology or medicine.
articles.body:
Take Nature ’s quiz on female Nobel laureates in physics, chemistry and physiology or medicine.
Since the Nobel prizes were first awarded in 1901, few women have been recognized in the categories of physics, chemistry and physiology or medicine.
The academies that award the prizes have acknowledged that women are under-represented among Nobel laureates, and have changed their nomination procedures to diversify the pool of winners .
But men still dominate the 125-year history of the awards.
In this year’s Nobel run-up, Nature shines a spotlight on female winners — and invites you to test your knowledge. This page covers data on Nobel prizewinners up to 2025; it will be updated with this year’s winners.
How many female science Nobel laureates can you name?
The first two prize entries have been filled in to get you started. Enter a surname or first name to make a guess. Click any revealed laureate to read about their work. You have ten minutes to answer while this page is visible.
Born in Poland as Maria Skłodowska, she later became a French citizen. She coined the term ‘radioactivity’ and shared half of the 1903 physics Nobel with her husband Pierre Curie for studies in radiation. She won the 1911 chemistry prize for her discoveries of polonium and radium (her husband died in 1906).
Credit: Henri Manuel. Nobel Foundation archive.

articles.title: Can we have class outside? Seven tips to breeze through outdoor lectures
articles.description: Advocates say that delivering lectures and presentations al fresco can energize students and provide them with a complete experience.
articles.body:
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Find a new job Save article View saved research Education researcher Lian Kasper (front) advises teachers to think of outdoor education as an experience.
Pedro Maria Abreu Ferreira spends a lot of time outside. It’s part of his job: he conducts long-term ecological studies at the Pró-Mata Nature Research and Conservation Center in the Serra Gaúcha region, Brazil. He also spends a lot of time outdoors when teaching classes, both at the centre and as a biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Porto Alegre, Brazil.
Although it can be breezy, being outside with students is not always a breeze. When it comes to fieldwork, transportation issues are pretty common — on the way back from a palaeoecology trip Ferreira and his team were delayed because of damage to their bus’ suspension. During a botany visit to the Pró-Mata reserve, he and his students experienced a strong, cold snap of weather known as a polar air mass. He even had to call off a trip to a mangrove forest once because of the sheer number of mosquitoes and horseflies. “It was absolutely impossible to teach or even think straight despite all the repellent and protective clothing we had on,” he remembers.
But, despite these hiccups, Ferreira thinks that the outdoor classroom is a must for teaching biology, and especially ecology. “Teaching outside is kind of mandatory, because you have to show the students what’s out there,” he says. “It’s more of a complete student experience.”
Although some regions are more conducive for al fresco teaching than others, it still provides a way to mix things up when working with students. Nature spoke to lecturers and outdoor-education coordinators about why it can be beneficial and how to prepare your students — and yourself — for the elements.
There are many ways to implement outdoor education in academia, explains Janne Fengler, who studies educational sciences and teacher training at the University of Luxembourg in Esch-sur-Alzette. As a member of the Outdoor Learning in Higher Education project, she and her colleagues are preparing a systematic analysis of outdoor education at universities and other education settings.
According to Fengler, there have been studies on the use of outdoor education in preschools, primary schools and secondary schools. But there has been less research on outdoor learning in higher education.
How to bring health and happiness to your lab

articles.title: ‘Vibe coding’ makes the dictionary: AI terms recognized by Merriam-Webster
articles.description: ‘Agentic’, ‘prompt engineering’ and other technical terms are among the 1,400 entries added to the online catalogue of the iconic lexicon.
articles.body:
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research Phrases such as ‘vibe coding’ have become widely used enough to merit entries in the Merriam-Webster dictionary. Credit: Brandon Bell/Getty
Artificial intelligence has achieved the ultimate sign of recognition: AI lingo has made it into the dictionary.
A slew of words and phrases about AI and technology has been added to the online version of the venerable Merriam-Webster dictionary, which has been a staple of US libraries and classrooms for decades and traces its roots back to a compendium of words published in 1806. Scholars say that the latest additions, which were announced in September and include terms such as ‘ agentic ’ and ‘natural language processing’, are notable for the advanced knowledge needed to understand them (see ‘Digital dictionary’).
“You can’t really explain ‘ vibe coding ’ if you don’t know what ‘programming’ is,” says Peter Sokolowski, a lexicographer at Merriam-Webster who writes and edits dictionary entries. He says that the sophistication of the newly listed words reflects non-specialists’ expanded access to highly technical terms, thanks to twenty-first-century digital communication.
“This particular batch, more than any other that I’ve seen, really does feel like it’s a meta-commentary on language,” says Sokolowski.
For a word to earn a spot in the Merriam-Webster dictionary, it must first appear repeatedly in mainstream media outlets such as newspapers and magazines, says Sokolowski. Specialist groups of physical- and biological-science ‘definers’ with expertise in these fields identify words that should be added. They then dive deeper into a word’s technical usage to understand its meaning and create a definition targeted at a general audience.
The Merriam-Webster dictionary, which traces its roots to a version published in the early nineteenth century, has added a host of technology-related terms.
Artificial-intelligence and computing terms
The surging number of complex technical words isn’t surprising, says Lera Boroditsky, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, San Diego, who studies language and cognition. Technological and scientific innovations often drive language change, she says, adding that today’s rate of technological advancement is comparable to, if not greater than, the rate seen during the industrial revolution. That rapid-fire change drives the generation of new words. “The more complex a society becomes, the more of these tightly packed units of meaning we have to make, so we can talk about things that are complex in ways that don't take forever,” she says.

articles.title: 2D semiconductor aims to turbocharge development of high-performance electronics
articles.description: An ultrathin semiconductor that conducts electricity using positively charged ‘holes’ might clear the way for next-generation electronic devices.
articles.body:
Taoyu Zou is in the Department of Chemical Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology, Pohang 37673, South Korea.
Yong-Young Noh is in the Department of Chemical Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology, Pohang 37673, South Korea.
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research Electric currents in semiconductors arise from the movement of either negatively charged electrons or positive charge carriers known as holes. Research into atomically thin semiconductors has yielded remarkable 2D materials that efficiently transport electrons. However, identifying counterpart materials that efficiently transport holes has been much more challenging. The lack of such materials has been a considerable obstacle to the implementation of complementary 2D electronics — in which devices that use electron-transporting (n-type) 2D semiconductors are paired with equivalent devices that use hole-transporting (p-type) 2D semiconductors to improve overall performance and power efficiency. Writing in Nature , Tseng et al . 1 report a semiconductor known as boron carbon nitride (BCN) that potentially fills this gap.

articles.title: Harmful tau spreads like self-propagating prion proteins
articles.description: Structural studies support the idea that fibrillized tau protein, a feature of neurodegenerative disorders, acts as a prion-like template to induce misfolding in healthy tau.
articles.body:
Kayleigh Mason-Chalmers is in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, the UCLA-DOE Institute for Genomics and Proteomics, and the STROBE NSF Science and Technology Center, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, California 90095, USA.
Jose A. Rodriguez is in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, the UCLA-DOE Institute for Genomics and Proteomics, and the STROBE NSF Science and Technology Center, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, California 90095, USA.
Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research Prions are shape-shifting, self-assembling proteins that transform from a physiologically harmless version into one that is misfolded, prone to aggregation and infectious. What makes prions and prion-like proteins capable of causing disease is their ability to act as templates, forcing normal functional proteins into a toxic form. Several proteins that are associated with neurodegenerative diseases, such as amyloid-β, α-synuclein and tau, are thought to spread in a prion-like manner 1 , 2 , but experimental support for some aspects of this hypothesis and its atomic basis have been lacking. In their paper in Nature , Lövestam et al. 3 show that injecting human tau fibrils into mice causes mouse tau to take on the form of the injected structures, bolstering the theory that tau propagates similarly to prions.
